title: Member, not part
hookLine: call yourself a member of humanity, not just a part, and you'll love from the heart (Meditations 7.13)

cards: A spare tire is part of a car. Take it out, put in another one, and the car doesn't notice. Your hand is not like that.
Cut it, and your whole body flinches; your other hand reaches over without being asked. Nobody has to remind it that it's on the same team.
Marcus Aurelius noticed that in Greek, the word for a replaceable piece and the word for a living limb differ by a single letter, and he built a whole lesson out of that letter.

teach.b: In Meditations seven, thirteen, Marcus says thinking beings are joined together like the limbs of one body, made to work with each other. That's an old Stoic picture of humanity: not a crowd of strangers, but one body.

In Greek, a limb or member is melos; a part, a piece, is meros. Only the middle letter changes: lambda becomes rho. If you call yourself merely a part, Marcus says, you don't yet love people from the heart.
Call yourself a member, a living limb, and something shifts. How do you know which you are? His test is sharp.
If doing good to others doesn't yet delight you for its own sake, if you do it only because it's right, as a duty, you're still thinking like a part.
A member helps the way your left hand helps your right: not as a favor, not to be thanked, because it's the same body. Marcus isn't scolding duty; doing good from duty is still good.

teach.h: KINDNESS AS CARE OF THE BODY.
teach.b: He's pointing past it, to a place where kindness feels like taking care of yourself, because it is. Many families know this.
You don't drive your sister to the airport because it's the correct thing. You drive her because she's your sister. Marcus asks what life would be like if the circle of sister were a lot wider.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes use the melos and meros wordplay as a reminder to help others as members of one body, the way one hand helps the other, rather than as a duty to be completed.

o: a living limb of one body, not a replaceable piece
a piece of a machine that can be swapped out
someone who has signed up and paid to join a club

games.q: member, not part — tap the pairs.

s: in Greek, member and part differ by one letter
melos and meros: lambda in one, rho in the other.
Marcus says doing good from duty is worthless
he points past duty to delight in doing good, without scolding duty.

games.q: you help a colleague, but it feels like a chore you're checking off. by 7.13, what does that suggest?
o: you're thinking like a part, not yet a member.
games.why: Meditations 7.13: if doing good doesn't yet delight you for its own sake, you still think of yourself as a part, meros, not a member, melos.

practice: Feel your two hands resting, and how easily they work together, without negotiation. Bring to mind someone outside your family, a coworker, a neighbor, a stranger you saw today, and hold them the way one hand holds the other.
Notice how that changes what you'd be willing to do for them.

wordCard.voice: Member. Marcus's one-letter lesson: not a replaceable part, but a living limb of one body, who loves from the heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a limb, a member of a body. Marcus contrasts it with μέρος (MEH-ros), a part.

carryVoice: Your line: a member. One body, and the circle a little wider. That's day five hundred eighty-seven.
